items.title: 56706_Buddy Tate oral history interview
items.q: So I was with Victoria Spivey, she had a review

ctx.x: Okay. Well, when -- this is after I joined the band. Well, King Oliver, I had listened to King Oliver's records and I would listen to Louie and he didn't move me like Louie. He could play, but this was before he developed pyorrhea and all of that. He could play, but his sound wasn't as fat and he didn't have as much punch and he didn't swing as much as Louie. And -- but of course, when I actually heard him in person, he had a big band, he was working out of an agency out of Shawnee, Oklahoma, and he came down to…

Then when I hear him again maybe three years later, Pres was with him, he was playing tenor with him. So I was with Victoria Spivey, she had a review, she had two million-dollar sellers, records, and she was in the first black picture that was produced by a big white production, you know, like King Vidor, and the picture was "Hallelujah" and it was ----- a pretty girl by the name of Nina Mae McKinney then, you know, she was in the picture and so was Victoria Spivey in the picture. So after she made the picture,…

So we went down there to jam and somebody told me, says, "King Oliver's here, upstairs. They just come in this morning. They got Red Young with them." They called Lester Red then, you know. So I had met Lester before when he played alto and his sister played tenor. So -- but that was back in '20s, back in Frankie Trumbauer time, when I met him, you know,

items.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: from T. Holder I worked with Victoria Spivey’s Tan Town Revue

ctx.x: I’d just like to open with a few questions. I’d like to ask you how did you first get attracted to the field of jazz? And how young were you when you started playing?

Well I must have been about 14, between 14 and 16 years of age. And we had a family band in my home town in Sherman, Texas. And it was a nice little old band, it was a good band, and we would play towns like, well I’d say from Sherman to we’d go to Oklahoma City and Ardmore, Oklahoma, and places like that. And my first professional band that I worked with was with a band called T. Holders Twelve Clouds of Joy, who later became Andy Kirk’s Twelve Clouds of Joy. And I left home with them when I was about, well…
traveling more until I had several health problems, and that cut off the traveling. So that’s where I am today, that’s about it.
